lead: This unit explains how to sense pressure, sound, acceleration, magnetic field, light, position and force with piezoelectric, Hall, magnetostrictive, optical and digital transducers. After it you can choose a sensor for a dynamic or optical measurement, design its basic signal conditioning, and read its data sheet limits.
about: This unit covers sensors that use piezoelectricity, magnetism, light and digital encoding. Chapter 4.1 starts with piezoelectric transducers and their charge amplifiers. Chapter 4.2 uses the same crystals for ultrasonic distance and flow sensing. Chapter 4.3 treats seismic mass accelerometers as second-order systems. Chapters 4.4 and 4.5 cover Hall and magnetostrictive sensors. Chapter 4.6 introduces photoelectric and fibre optic sensing. Chapter 4.7 explains digital encoders. Chapters 4.8 and 4.9 are advanced topics in speed and force-balance measurement. Chapter 4.10 covers phototubes and photomultipliers, and Chapter 4.11 covers semiconductor photodevices and spectrophotometry.

chapters.idea: A piezoelectric crystal makes charge when pressed and changes shape when driven, so it measures dynamic force, pressure and vibration and sends or receives ultrasound.
chapters.depth: Direct and inverse piezoelectric effect; charge coefficient d in C/N or pC/N, voltage coefficient g in V·m/N; quartz, PZT and PVDF; equivalent circuit as a charge source with parallel capacitance and leakage resistance; charge amplifier, voltage amplifier, cable capacitance, low-frequency cut-off; use as a pressure transducer and as an ultrasound transmitter or receiver. Some syllabi call g the voltage sensitivity.

figure.aria: A piezoelectric crystal feeds a charge amplifier, then a filter, then the output; the charge amplifier is the key high-impedance block.

chapters.example: A quartz disc of area 2 cm² and thickness 1 mm has d = 2.3 pC/N and εr = 4.5. A force of 10 N is applied. Find the charge and the open-circuit voltage. Q = dF = 2.3 pC/N × 10 N = 23 pC. C = ε0 εr A / t = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m × 4.5 × 2×10⁻⁴ m² / 1×10⁻³ m = 7.97×10⁻¹² F ≈ 8 pF. V = Q / C = 23×10⁻¹² C / 7.97×10⁻¹² F = 2.9 V.
chapters.trap: Do not use a piezoelectric sensor for a steady force: the charge leaks away, so the reading falls to zero.
chapters.leave: Ultrasound propagation to 4.2; charge-amplifier design to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Ultrasonic sensors send sound above 20 kHz and listen for the echo; the delay gives distance, level or flow, and acoustic sensors measure sound pressure.
chapters.depth: Speed of sound in air about 343 m/s at 20 °C; wavelength λ = v / f; pulse-echo and time of flight; beam angle and resolution; piezoelectric and capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducers; through-beam and reflective acoustic sensors; applications parking aid, level, flow and non-destructive testing; Doppler flow. Some syllabi call this the ultrasound transducer topic.

figure.aria: A transmitter sends a pulse to a target, the receiver catches the echo, and a timer converts time of flight to distance.

chapters.example: A parking sensor sends a 40 kHz pulse. The echo returns after 12 ms. Speed of sound is 343 m/s. Find the distance to the obstacle. d = v t / 2 = 343 m/s × 0.012 s / 2 = 2.058 m ≈ 2.06 m.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the factor 2 gives twice the true distance.
chapters.leave: Capacitor microphone to Unit 3; echo signal processing to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A seismic mass on a spring and damper measures vibration: below resonance it reads acceleration, above resonance it reads displacement.
chapters.depth: Second-order mass-spring-damper; natural frequency fn = (1/2π)√(k/m), where k is spring constant and m is seismic mass; damping ratio ζ; amplitude ratio and phase; accelerometer use f << fn; seismometer use f >> fn; piezoelectric accelerometer, capacitive MEMS accelerometer; charge amplifier; mounting resonance; applications airbag, machine vibration and earthquake sensing.

figure.aria: Amplitude ratio of a seismic mass against frequency ratio for damping ratios 0.1 and 0.7; the low-frequency part is flat for the accelerometer.

chapters.example: An accelerometer has natural frequency 10 kHz and damping ratio 0.7. Find the amplitude error at 1 kHz. r = f / fn = 1000 / 10000 = 0.1. H = 1 / √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) = 1 / √((0.99)² + (0.14)²) = 1 / √0.9997 = 1.00015. The reading is 0.015 % high.
chapters.trap: Using an accelerometer near its natural frequency gives a large, phase-shifted output.
chapters.leave: Strain-gauge accelerometers to Unit 2; MEMS fabrication to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A magnetic field pushes the current carriers in a thin semiconductor strip to one side, creating a Hall voltage proportional to the field.
chapters.depth: Hall voltage VH = RH I B / t, where RH = 1/(n e) is the Hall coefficient, I is current, B is flux density, t is thickness, n is carrier density and e is electron charge; current drive and voltage drive; InSb, GaAs and silicon; sensitivity; linear sensor and threshold switch; offset and temperature drift; applications position, gear-tooth speed, current clamp and compass.

figure.aria: A current source drives a Hall plate, a differential amplifier picks up the small Hall voltage, and a comparator gives a switch output.

chapters.example: An InSb Hall plate has RH = 3.8×10⁻⁴ m³/C and thickness 0.1 mm. A current of 10 mA flows in a field of 0.2 T. Find VH. t = 0.1 mm = 1×10⁻⁴ m. VH = RH I B / t = 3.8×10⁻⁴ × 0.01 A × 0.2 T / 1×10⁻⁴ m = 7.6×10⁻³ V = 7.6 mV.
chapters.trap: The Hall coefficient is not the same as the sensitivity in volts per tesla; thickness and current set the output.
chapters.leave: Magnetostrictive sensors to 4.5; amplifier design to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Magnetic materials change length in a magnetic field and change magnetization under stress, so they sense force, torque and position and make sound waves.
chapters.depth: Joule magnetostriction, Villari effect and Wiedemann effect; magnetostrictive materials nickel, Metglas and Terfenol-D; bias field; magneto-elastic torque sensor; magnetostrictive delay line; ultrasonic transducer; advantages of ruggedness and high force; hysteresis.

figure.aria: Two paths: a drive coil strains a magnetostrictive rod, and an input force changes the rod magnetization to give a pickup-coil voltage.

chapters.example: A Terfenol-D rod is 50 mm long. At a bias field its magnetostriction is 1200 ppm. Find the change in length. 1200 ppm = 1200×10⁻⁶. ΔL = λ L = 1200×10⁻⁶ × 50 mm = 0.060 mm = 60 μm.
chapters.trap: Magnetostriction is not linear without a bias field; hysteresis can make the same stress give different outputs.
chapters.leave: Hall sensors to 4.4; smart materials to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Photoelectric sensors turn light into an electrical signal, and fibre optic sensors guide light so that strain, temperature or pressure changes the light.
chapters.depth: Photoelectric effect; through-beam, retroreflective and diffuse sensors; fibre structure core and cladding, total internal reflection, numerical aperture; intensity-modulated fibre sensor; mention of fibre Bragg grating; advantages of immunity to electrical noise; applications counting, safety, temperature and strain.

figure.aria: An LED launches light into a fibre, a sensor head modulates it, and a photodiode plus amplifier turns the received light into a reading.

chapters.example: A fibre optic link launches 1 mW and receives 0.2 mW after 2 km. Find the loss in dB and in dB/km. Loss = 10 log10(1 / 0.2) = 10 log10 5 = 6.99 dB ≈ 7 dB. Loss per km = 7 dB / 2 km = 3.5 dB/km.
chapters.trap: A fibre sensor measures the change in light, not the light itself; source drift can look like a measurement change.
chapters.leave: Photodiode and phototransistor details to 4.11; phototube to 4.10.

chapters.idea: A position encoder turns displacement into a digital code or pulse count, so the reading is exact and easy to send.
chapters.depth: Incremental encoder A and B channels and index; quadrature gives four counts per slot; absolute encoder binary and Gray code; linear scale and rotary disc; resolution = 360° / N or pitch / 4, where N is slots per revolution; magnetic and optical types; applications CNC, printers and robotics.

figure.title: 3-bit Gray code track
figure.aria: A 3-bit Gray code track with three rows and eight positions; only one bit changes between adjacent positions.

chapters.example: A rotary incremental encoder has 1000 slots per revolution and uses quadrature decoding. Find the counts per revolution and the resolution in degrees. Counts = 4 × 1000 = 4000 counts/rev. Resolution = 360° / 4000 = 0.09°.
chapters.trap: Counting only channel A gives one quarter of the available resolution and no direction.
chapters.leave: Capacitive proximity to Unit 3; digital filtering to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Speed can be measured from a generator voltage, from a stroboscope flash that freezes the shaft, or from the frequency of a signal.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. DC and AC tachogenerators; output voltage proportional to speed; ripple and filtering; stroboscope principle and aliasing; variable-frequency sensors such as vibrating-wire or oscillator sensors; frequency-to-voltage conversion.

figure.aria: A shaft drives a tachogenerator; its AC output is rectified and filtered to a DC voltage that reads speed.

chapters.example: A DC tachogenerator has a constant of 0.05 V per rad/s. Find the output at 1500 rpm. 1500 rpm = 1500 × 2π / 60 = 157.08 rad/s. V = 0.05 V/(rad/s) × 157.08 rad/s = 7.85 V.
chapters.trap: A stroboscope can show a stationary image at a submultiple of the true speed, so check for aliasing.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 dynamic characteristics; basic electromagnetic induction.
chapters.leave: Optical encoders to 4.7; motor drives to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A force-balance transducer uses feedback to cancel the input force with a coil force, so the coil current becomes an accurate measure of force or pressure.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Servo loop, displacement detector, error amplifier, coil in a magnetic gap, feedback force, current output; closed-loop linearity; response speed and stability; applications pressure transmitter, weighing and accelerometer.

figure.aria: An input force bends a beam; a displacement sensor and amplifier drive a coil that pushes back on the beam, closing the force-balance loop.

chapters.example: A force-balance pressure transmitter balances a 2 N input force with a coil of total conductor length 50 m in a gap flux density 0.25 T. Find the coil current. F = B I L, so I = F / (B L) = 2 N / (0.25 T × 50 m) = 2 / 12.5 = 0.16 A.
chapters.trap: The accuracy depends on the feedback loop, not on the spring; an open-loop test gives the wrong answer.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6 amplifiers and feedback; Unit 1 static characteristics.
chapters.leave: Pressure sensor construction to Unit 3; control theory to later courses.

chapters.idea: A phototube converts light into electrons; a photomultiplier tube multiplies those electrons with dynodes; a scintillation counter first turns radiation into light for the PMT.
chapters.depth: Phototube photocathode and anode; vacuum; photomultiplier tube dynode chain, gain δⁿ, transit time, dark current; scintillation materials such as NaI(Tl); photoelectron; pulse counting; applications radiation survey, medical imaging and spectroscopy.

figure.aria: A photon hits a photocathode, the emitted electron is multiplied by dynodes, and the anode pulse is counted.

chapters.example: A PMT has 10 dynodes and each dynode multiplies by 4. Find the total gain and the anode charge for 100 photoelectrons. Gain = 4¹⁰ = 1,048,576. Anode electrons = 100 × 1,048,576 = 1.048576×10⁸. Charge = 1.048576×10⁸ × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C = 1.68×10⁻¹¹ C.
chapters.trap: The gain is δⁿ, not nδ; dark current also gets multiplied.
chapters.leave: Semiconductor photodiodes to 4.11; pulse counting circuits to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Semiconductor photodevices change current or resistance with light, and spectrophotometers use this to measure concentration from absorption.
chapters.depth: Photodiode reverse bias, PIN and avalanche types, responsivity in A/W, dark current; phototransistor gain; photovoltaic cell; photoconductive cell or LDR; spectral response; comparison of photoelectric transducers; spectrophotometer with source, monochromator, sample and detector; Beer-Lambert law A = ε c l, where A is absorbance, ε is molar absorptivity, c is concentration and l is path length; applications.

figure.aria: A light source passes through a monochromator and sample, and a detector plus readout gives absorbance at the chosen wavelength.

chapters.example: A spectrophotometer reads absorbance A = 0.30 in a 1 cm cell. The molar absorptivity is 1500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. Find the concentration. c = A / (ε l) = 0.30 / (1500 × 1) = 2.0×10⁻⁴ mol/L.
chapters.trap: Absorbance is logarithmic; doubling the concentration does not double A unless the solution stays in the linear range.
chapters.prereq: 4.6 photoelectric and fibre sensors; basic semiconductor junction.
chapters.leave: Phototube and PMT to 4.10; fibre sensing to 4.6.
